summary:
Indonesia is a high-risk destination for trans visitors. The national penal code signed in December 2022 took effect on 2 January 2026 and penalises consensual extra-marital sex between adults with up to two years' imprisonment. Because same-sex marriage is not permitted in Indonesia, this provision effectively criminalises all consensual same-sex relations; Outright International reports that prosecutions are selective rather than systematic.

The Human Dignity Trust country profile records that two provinces, Aceh and South Sumatra, criminalise same-sex sexual activity between men and between women, alongside national-level provisions targeting morality. In Aceh, where Sharia law applies, two men were publicly caned for a same-sex relationship in February 2025. Aceh's punishments are imposed under provincial religious law and reach anyone present in the province, including foreign visitors.

Official hostility has moved into national security policy. In October 2025 President Prabowo Subianto issued a presidential decree declaring the spread of LGBTQ culture a non-military national threat, placing it alongside separatism and terrorism. Reporting by The Diplomat in August 2026 and by ABC News days later links that framing to a surge in vigilante attacks on transgender women, with an academic commentator stating that the regulation moves hostile rhetoric into the official doctrine of national defence policy, defining LGBTQ people as risks to be monitored and controlled.

Police action against gatherings is documented. On 22 June 2025 officers raided a privately rented villa in the Puncak area near Bogor following public reports of a 'gay party' and arrested 75 people, 74 men and one woman. Amnesty International's Deputy Director Wirya Adiwena called the operation a blatant violation of human rights and privacy and stated that the gathering violated no law.

Custody carries demonstrable lethal risk. In August 2022 Rodrigo Ventocilla, a Harvard student on honeymoon in Bali, was arrested at an Indonesian airport on drug charges; during a WhatsApp call his mother in Lima was told authorities demanded up to US$100,000 for his release. He died in custody. His mother alleges police beat him, while Indonesian police denied that violence was used.

Document rules are restrictive but not closed. Transgender Indonesians may change legal gender on official documents after sex reassignment surgery and a judge's approval, after which they may marry someone of the opposite legal gender. Since June 2021 the Ministry of Home Affairs has run outreach to issue identification papers (Kartu Tanda Penduduk) to transgender people across multiple provinces including Banten, West Java, Central Java, East Java, North Sumatra, South Sumatra, South Sulawesi, Lampung and Papua, because many were undocumented, particularly where families disapproved, leaving them without work or social services. Only 'male' and 'female' sex descriptors exist, with no third gender or X marker, and a transgender person's gender at birth is printed unless court recognition has already been obtained.

Expression about homosexuality and gender identity is criminalised or blocked. The 2006 Law Against Pornography and Pornoaction penalises any writing or audio-visual presentation showing or suggesting same-sex relations with up to seven years' imprisonment, and in March 2016 the national broadcasting commission banned television and radio programmes presenting LGBTQ behaviour as normal. The government has banned websites and apps containing 'gay' or LGBTQ-related terms, including Grindr, and shut down the Instagram account of the comic Alpantuni; in 2025 a new bill was under discussion to prohibit online content presenting lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender behaviour.

Protection machinery exists on paper. As of 2019 no specific law protects Indonesian citizens from discrimination or harassment based on sexual orientation or gender identity. The police have issued a circular since 2015 for processing hate speech related to sexual orientation and gender identity, and Regulation of the Head of National Police Number 8 of 2009 stipulates a duty to protect minority groups' special rights including sexual orientation.
tangentialFactors:
The escalation described in August 2026 is presented by The Diplomat and ABC News as continuous with officials' verbal attacks rather than a sudden outbreak, with the October 2025 presidential decree treated as the point where political rhetoric became defence policy. Both outlets frame violence and official framing as one development, which matters for visitors assessing whether hostility is spontaneous or state-encouraged.

Human Rights Watch has documented discriminatory regulations, arrests and criminal trials against LGBT people in Indonesia since 2016, a decade-long record that predates the current penal code. The pattern indicates that enforcement risk accumulates over time rather than depending on any single statute.

Censorship measures are unusually specific and affect what a visitor may read, post or download. Website and application bans, the removal of a comic's social media account, and a 2025 bill targeting online content sit alongside the seven-year pornography penalty, so digital expression carries its own exposure separate from conduct.

Custody allegations in the Ventocilla case concern a foreign national and a drug arrest at an airport, which places arrival screening and detention within the risk picture rather than leaving it at the level of local policing.
localsOnly:
Jakarta's Social Agency has declared transgender women (waria) 'socially dysfunctional' since 2018, conducts regular raids, and takes detained transgender people to city-owned 'rehabilitation' centres where they are held alongside homeless people and released only after signing a promise not to repeat their 'offence'. Officials have stated the measure is intended as a deterrent against being transgender.

Conversion therapy is widely practised and openly advertised in rehabilitation centres, and includes corrective rape by family members against lesbian women. LGBTQ groups are working on safe houses and evacuation plans. The Yayasan Srikandi Sejati organization runs a free health clinic providing HIV/AIDS counselling and free condoms to transgender sex workers, and Yogyakarta hosts the only madrasa for transgender people in the world.

Human Rights Watch reported on 7 July 2026 a surge in abuse against LGBT students following officials' condemnations of a student group at Universitas Indonesia. Arus Pelangi, Indonesia's LGBT umbrella organization, documented 94 cases, and in early July officials called on parents to monitor children in 'this lifestyle'.

Institutional hostility has a documented origin point. An August 2016 Human Rights Watch report recorded that the Indonesian Psychiatric Association proclaimed same-sex orientation and transgender identities 'mental illnesses' and recommended psychological 'rehabilitation', while the Jokowi government remained mostly silent.

Workplace and employment protection is theoretical. Protection against discriminatory employment practices on any ground is guaranteed in the Constitution and in Human Rights Law (No. 39/1999), but the Attorney General's Office rescinded a public job offer that declared LGBTQ persons need not apply after advice from the National Commission on Human Rights. A police brigadier identified as TT was fired for being gay after colleagues outed him, and his lawsuit was rejected by the Semarang State Administrative Court in May 2019 on procedural grounds.
outOfScopeNotes:
The source inventory does not establish whether the penal code's extra-marital sex provision has yet been used to prosecute a foreign visitor, and reporting describes prosecution as selective without specifying arrest or conviction figures for tourists.

No official travel advisory from any foreign government is included here, so the risk assessment rests on reporting and human rights documentation rather than on a state department's current guidance. Whether such advisories currently mention the January 2026 penal code or the October 2025 presidential decree is unresolved.

The reach of Aceh's caning beyond provincial boundaries for visitors transiting or in transit is not addressed: the sources confirm that the February 2025 caning was imposed under provincial religious law, but do not set out whether the national government can extradite or transfer a foreign national to Aceh.

The scope of the pending 2025 online content bill is unresolved. Sources state it was under discussion to prohibit content presenting LGBT behaviour, but do not record whether it has been enacted, its penalties, or whether it applies to material viewed on a visitor's own device.

Whether the seven-year pornography penalty has been applied against foreign nationals for online content is not documented in the inventory, and the interaction between document rules for legal gender change and entry screening for foreign IDs is not sourced.
